title: Sana and the Thinking Pause
markdown:
Teacher Jae’s voice chimed, “Time for Codeball!” Sana’s Quick Reflex app tracked every move. “Let’s smash our record with super-speedy dodges,” she cheered. The classroom buzzed.

A stray ball zipped toward a shelf of glass beakers. The app flashed COLLISION IMMINENT. Instead of a dodge — crack. Beakers tumbled, landing safely on padded mats, which Jae had insisted on after last term’s optimism. Tern the gull squawked, feathers puffed, a critic with wings.

“Whoa.” Sana stared at her screen. “Quick Reflex didn’t do anything. It should have seen that coming.”

Jae walked over, calm. “A close call. The app missed. Interesting. It shows us something about how we work, not only how code fails.”

Later Jae held a bouncy ball. Tern hopped onto a desk, watching with the focus of someone who believed all balls were tribute. “Imagine this is unexpected.” They tossed it. Instantly Tern’s head flicked. He caught it. Squawk.

“Tern didn’t think. Eyes saw it. Body reacted. A reflex. Super-quick highways. Emergency shortcuts.”

Jae picked up a stick. “Now this stick is in the way of a berry. To get the berry I decide to reach. I plan the stretch. Then the brain sends a slower signal.” They moved an arm slowly, theatrical on purpose. “A conscious decision. Longer, because thinking takes the scenic route.”

Sana’s eyes widened. “The ball was so fast Quick Reflex didn’t have enough time. It tried to process a surprise as if I needed to think. It needed a reflex, like Tern. A different signal.”

“Your app makes planned movements fast. Sometimes the world throws surprises that trigger old reflexes. The app needs to notice those sudden moments and switch systems. A little thinking time for emergencies — or it will optimise us straight into the glass.”

Sana’s pencil flew. “A safety pause. If Quick Reflex sees a collision coming, send a different signal. Not only move fast. Pause. Figure it out. Then react.”

For days she tinkered, Tern supervising from the lamp and occasionally deleting a semicolon with his beak. Finally she called Jae. “Done. High chance of collision triggers a tiny pause — a blink — so the brain can choose. Thinking time when we need it most.”

Jae tested. A virtual ball zoomed at a virtual beaker. A thinking-brain icon blinked. Virtual players shifted, missed the crash. Tern cooed, which in Tern meant the maths had passed the feather exam.

Jae nodded at the icon, then at the mats. “Automatic and thoughtful. Fast roads and slow ones. You made the tech safer by admitting both exist.”

Sana grinned. She did not wonder what else brains did in secret. She versioned the build safety-pause-1, taped a note to the beaker shelf that said the mats are not a personality, and let Tern keep the bouncy ball on the condition he practised catching it over the cushion, not the glass.
